newsitem.title: USA: General says U.S. troops did not get CIA warning.
newsitem.headline: General says U.S. troops did not get CIA warning.

text.p: The CIA said on Wednesday that, despite mistakes, it had warned U.S. Gulf War forces of possible chemical weapons at an Iraqi munitions dump before it was blown sky high.
But a U.S. general who helped demolish the facility said that warning did not get to the troops.
When asked at a congressional hearing how he felt about the miscommunication, Maj. Gen. Robert Flowers replied: "Well, I'm disappointed."
He said U.S. Army engineers would have taken far more stringent safety precautions if they had been warned of possible war gas at the site.
Flowers was called out of the audience to give the surprise testimony to two House Veterans Affairs subcomittees.

A CIA official testified at the hearing that, despite mistakes, the spy agency did warn the military of possible chemical weapons at the Kamisiyah weapons dump. A Defence Department official said the warning did get to some Gulf War units' headquarters.

The Defence Department announced last summer that about 20,000 U.S. troops were in the area and so may have been exposed to chemical weapons, although there is no hard evidence so far that any were in fact exposed.

The CIA admitted at a news conference last week that it had solid intelligence by 1986 of chemical weapons at Kamisiyah, but did not find that report and give it to U.S. military forces when the Gulf War erupted.

But CIA official Robert Walpole said at the hearing that the CIA and the Defence Intelligence Agency each warned U.S. forces in Saudi Arabia of the possibility of chemical weapons just days before the Kamisiyah dump was demolished.

He said the CIA warning was the previously disclosed Feb. 23, 1991, cable to Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf's Gulf War command nine days before the demolition that did not name Kamisiyah but gave coordinates for it and said there was "possible CW," meaning chemical weapons there.
Walpole said at the news conference last week that an unidentified U.S. ambassador was given that information, which originated from someone in the Iranian Air Force or defence industry.

He said the second warning was sent by the Defence Department's DIA on Feb. 28, about four days before the demolition, that biological and chemical weapons could be stored at Kamisiyah and other sites.

The Pentagon's special assistant for Gulf War illnesses, Dr. Bernard Rostker, said Schwarzkopf's headquarters did order a check of Kamisiyah for chemical weapons and did relay the warning to at least some Gulf War units' headquarters.
"The military did not just sit on this," he said.
But he said before Gen. Flowers' surprise testimony that defence investigators had not been able to trace whether the troops that blew up the Iraqi dump were given the warning.
"It may well be that they were," Rostker said. "We just can't certify that at this time."

Rostker said about 300 of the 20,000 troops near Kamisiyah reported a variety of health problems, and the Pentagon has not ruled out chemical exposure as one possible cause of unexplained illnesses suffered by thousands of Gulf War veterans.
Flowers, now commander of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in the Mississippi Valley, was a colonel at the time and commander of one of the Army engineer units that blew up the Kamisiyah dump.
He said they had no warning of chemical weapons at the dump and said that when he asked if it had been checked for the presence of chemical weapons he was told it had.
Flowers said instruments did not detect chemical weapons at the time and there was no sign, such as illness among the troops, of such weapons.
He said he simply does not know whether they were exposed to chemical weapons.
